compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same set of services, the same group of regular customers, the same authority and budget, the same launch date. If one person owns the shop and the other was asked for a quick opinion, their different responsibilities can explain which questions they raise.

| The same event (one price list, the same regular customers) | ENTP: the basis more likely attended to | ESFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A three-tier draft arrives | Whether the distance between tiers and the choosing path read clearly at a glance | Whether the tier names and wording make regulars feel ranked | Structure and customer comprehension; either can check both |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a small shop that has just started to do well, both may strike up conversation with customers, and both may wear a flat expression through an evening of rush orders. The shared E only says attention and energy turn outward more often; it guarantees neither warmth nor remembering names. How much someone chats comes from habit, training and the state of the day.

The difference sits in which face of the same thing gets noticed. One more often looks at what other approaches could work, and whether the structure could flow better; the other more often looks at how the specific people in the room are doing, and how this was handled before. Both kinds of attention appear; the difference is which is taken first more often.

### The price list on the table: both kinds of imagining appear

With the same price list, either may think first on behalf of new customers: how the three tiers differ, whether the middle one is worth it, whether it reads clearly at a glance. Either may also think first on behalf of existing customers: one price has become three, will some feel demoted, and what do we tell the people renewing at the old price. Which side is raised first depends on the role, the information in hand and the last complaint or compliment, with no fixed correspondence to four letters.

What can be compared is the reason. Someone who more often cites "does the choice structure hold up" tends to be calculating tier gaps and looking for anchors; someone who more often cites "will commitments already made be broken" tends to be checking contracts and thinking through a transition. Both reasons can sit in the same discussion, and the same person may raise both in sequence.

The costs sit on both sides. Calculating only the structure may end with existing customers at the door asking "so I have been downgraded?"; attending only to the transition may produce three tiers none of which is worth buying, and the price increase fails. Which side is more likely to go wrong depends on how much of this shop's revenue comes from regulars and whether a price was ever promised, not on anyone's type.

### Why four identical functions read as two different people

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si and ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti. Moving the first two entries to the end gives the other stack: ENTP's Ne is third in ESFJ and Ti fourth; ESFJ's Fe is third in ENTP and Si fourth. The order within each pair stays the same.

The four processes fall into a perceiving group and a judging group. ENTP leads with a perceiving process (Ne), paired with a judging process (Ti). ESFJ leads with a judging process (Fe), paired with a perceiving process (Si). These are positions in the model. They cannot predict the order of actions, creativity or consideration for others.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: some give only the function name for ENTP's Fe and ESFJ's Ne without settling the attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and cannot be used to infer when someone finally thinks of other people. Both base descriptions are the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp) and the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are fictional pricing and engagement discussions, covering communication, the organisation of information and the division of work only, not legal, financial or contractual judgement. Real pricing decisions follow your own operating data and professional advice.

When two people work together, friction tends to appear when one is already changing the tiers and the other is still working out how to raise it with regulars. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each handles first. The division can be written down by duty and authority: who owns which part, who has the final signature. Writing it is more reliable than relying on rapport.

### The three tiers: should the middle tier offer less value?

(Fictional scene.) One set of services splits into basic at 99, standard at 199, premium at 399. Early in the discussion someone proposes making 199 visibly poor value, adding only two trivial features over 99, so customers either stay at 99 or jump to 399. The other objects: regulars renewing at a single price are using something close to 199, and turning that into the bad-value tier tells them they have been overpaying for years.

Set the goal first, then the tiers. This time the goal is for most new customers to land on 199: 99 moves volume at thin margin, 399 is a high threshold for a new customer, and the team wants to test whether customers see 199 as good value. With that goal, 199 has to stand up: the added service needs a clear purpose and enough use to justify the price difference of 100; 399 exists as a reference, with clearly wider entitlements and a jump in price, so that 199 looks like the reasonable choice rather than the tier being pushed.

"Will customers move from 199 to 399, and why" is a hypothesis to be tested, known only from the choice distribution and renewal feedback after launch; it cannot be written into the design as a goal, and cannot be engineered by making the middle tier bad.

Both risks are real: a structure that is too clever will feel like a trick once customers see it; attending only to regulars' feelings may leave all three tiers untouched and the increase unrealised. The middle path is to make 199 solid while giving regulars a transition period with written conditions, rather than using the middle tier as both a decoy and the main product.

The check is an exploratory interview, not a vote: ask five or six regulars to look at two versions of the list, with and without 199, and say which they would choose, why, which entitlement they did not understand, and what is missing now. What is recorded is reasons and sticking points; there is no threshold of "if this many people mention it, add it", and a sample this small cannot justify cutting or adding a tier. The interviews inform the price list; they do not judge anyone's type.

### A classmate's shop asks for pricing help: charge or not

(Fictional scene.) A university classmate has opened a small shop and asks you to look at the price list and the menu structure, saying several times "no rush, whenever you have time".

Either may simply produce a version, and either may ask about scope first. This is closer to a difference in task scope and relationship terms: whether there is time, whether this will recur, and how you and this classmate usually deal with each other all change the approach.

Put the same set of questions to both: how far does this help go, what is delivered, when is it needed, is there a fee, and does a later price change count as a new engagement. One more often checks whether a rule can be applied consistently — free this time, so is it free for the next person who asks; saying "one verbal opinion, implementation billed separately" saves both sides trouble. The other more often starts from the existing relationship — it is not easy for a classmate to ask, so hold the atmosphere first and find a moment to state the boundary. Both reasons can hold at once, and often appear in the same person.

A workable approach is layered: free this time, one verbal opinion, no documents; for implementation, a separate engagement with scope, deliverables, timing and fee written down.

Counterexamples worth remembering: some ENTPs will insist on a simple letter of engagement, and some ESFJs will take on three months of work with "we are classmates". Type does not decide who has better judgement about boundaries; whether the scope can be stated clearly depends on experience, the relationship and the situation. If the two take it on together, divide by who knows how, who has time and who is authorised to speak outward — not by four letters.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The most common thing taken as evidence is "who is better at conversation". Both can carry a dinner table, and both can stay silent all evening when tired. Chatting is habit and occasion; the shared E describes direction only, not warmth.

The second is dividing them by "who is better with people". ESFJ can speak very hard when interests are at stake, and ENTP can soothe someone sentence by sentence when it is needed. Treating "good at caring for people" as a type marker is wrong almost every time.

The third is treating seating as rank. Calling ENTP "not grounded" and ESFJ "no opinions of their own" turns a processing order into a defect. Four identical names only mean this writing uses the same vocabulary in a different order; nothing follows about who is better at ideas or more practical, or whose judgement is more reliable.

The fourth is treating J as "likes making plans" and P as "likes changing them". J/P is whether outer life forms an arrangement or keeps options; the same person can build a detailed schedule in a familiar field and improvise in an unfamiliar one, which has more to do with how settled the situation is.

(Fictional scene.) One set of services splits into basic at 99, standard at 199, premium at 399. Early in the discussion someone proposes making 199 visibly poor value, adding only two trivial features over 99, so customers either stay at 99 or jump to 399. The other objects: regulars renewing at a single price are using something close to 199, and turning that into the bad-value tier tells them they have been overpaying for years.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: In a small shop that has just started to do well, both may strike up conversation with customers, and both may wear a flat expression through an evening of rush orders. The shared E only says attention and energy turn outward more often; it guarantees neither warmth nor remembering names. How much someone chats comes from habit, training and the state of the day.

The difference sits in which face of the same thing gets noticed. One more often looks at what other approaches could work, and whether the structure could flow better; the other more often looks at how the specific people in the room are doing, and how this was handled before. Both kinds of attention appear; the difference is which is taken first more often.
### The price list on the table: both kinds of imagining appear

With the same price list, either may think first on behalf of new customers: how the three tiers differ, whether the middle one is worth it, whether it reads clearly at a glance. Either may also think first on behalf of existing customers: one price has become three, will some feel demoted, and what do we tell the people renewing at the old price. Which side is raised first depends on the role, the information in hand and the last complaint or compliment, with no fixed correspondence to four letters.

What can be compared is the reason. Someone who more often cites "does the choice structure hold up" tends to be calculating tier gaps and looking for anchors; someone who more often cites "will commitments already made be broken" tends to be checking contracts and thinking through a transition. Both reasons can sit in the same discussion, and the same person may raise both in sequence.

The costs sit on both sides. Calculating only the structure may end with existing customers at the door asking "so I have been downgraded?"; attending only to the transition may produce three tiers none of which is worth buying, and the price increase fails. Which side is more likely to go wrong depends on how much of this shop's revenue comes from regulars and whether a price was ever promised, not on anyone's type.
### Why four identical functions read as two different people

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si and ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti. Moving the first two entries to the end gives the other stack: ENTP's Ne is third in ESFJ and Ti fourth; ESFJ's Fe is third in ENTP and Si fourth. The order within each pair stays the same.

The four processes fall into a perceiving group and a judging group. ENTP leads with a perceiving process (Ne), paired with a judging process (Ti). ESFJ leads with a judging process (Fe), paired with a perceiving process (Si). These are positions in the model. They cannot predict the order of actions, creativity or consideration for others.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: some give only the function name for ENTP's Fe and ESFJ's Ne without settling the attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and cannot be used to infer when someone finally thinks of other people. Both base descriptions are the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp) and the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj).

body: The premise is aligned conditions: the same set of services, the same group of regular customers, the same authority and budget, the same launch date. If one person owns the shop and the other was asked for a quick opinion, their different responsibilities can explain which questions they raise.
Align the conditions before reading: the same event, the same information, the same deadline. Both types can use the other's approach; the table contrasts criteria either person could use.

| The same event (one price list, the same regular customers) | ENTP: the basis more likely attended to | ESFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A three-tier draft arrives | Whether the distance between tiers and the choosing path read clearly at a glance | Whether the tier names and wording make regulars feel ranked | Structure and customer comprehension; either can check both |
| What the middle tier adds over the basic one | Would the added service justify the same price difference under consistent criteria across all tiers? | How would that price difference affect regulars who rely on the added service, given what they were promised? | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| A regular says "it was not this price before" | Apply the same transition criteria to customers with comparable purchases | Weigh how the same transition options affect customers who relied on the previous price | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Competitors offer only two tiers | How to explain the differentiation, and which tier serves as the reference | Whether customers will find the options complicated, and whether the wording should be simplified | Positioning and decision cost; either can check with real customer feedback |
| Whether to raise prices across the board | Apply the same viability criteria to the same proposed increases | Weigh how the same increases would affect customers and what was promised to them | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The first week after launch | Keep several ways of responding open while the same launch data comes in | Agree on a provisional date and format for reviewing the same launch data | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. Someone who has priced a shop for years more often calculates the tier gaps first, and the other person touching a price list for the first time may only ask "is this too expensive"; the same person also switches approach depending on how much data is available and how tight the deadline is.

body: Scope note: the two passages below are fictional pricing and engagement discussions, covering communication, the organisation of information and the division of work only, not legal, financial or contractual judgement. Real pricing decisions follow your own operating data and professional advice.

When two people work together, friction tends to appear when one is already changing the tiers and the other is still working out how to raise it with regulars. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each handles first. The division can be written down by duty and authority: who owns which part, who has the final signature. Writing it is more reliable than relying on rapport.
### The three tiers: should the middle tier offer less value?

(Fictional scene.) One set of services splits into basic at 99, standard at 199, premium at 399. Early in the discussion someone proposes making 199 visibly poor value, adding only two trivial features over 99, so customers either stay at 99 or jump to 399. The other objects: regulars renewing at a single price are using something close to 199, and turning that into the bad-value tier tells them they have been overpaying for years.

Set the goal first, then the tiers. This time the goal is for most new customers to land on 199: 99 moves volume at thin margin, 399 is a high threshold for a new customer, and the team wants to test whether customers see 199 as good value. With that goal, 199 has to stand up: the added service needs a clear purpose and enough use to justify the price difference of 100; 399 exists as a reference, with clearly wider entitlements and a jump in price, so that 199 looks like the reasonable choice rather than the tier being pushed.

"Will customers move from 199 to 399, and why" is a hypothesis to be tested, known only from the choice distribution and renewal feedback after launch; it cannot be written into the design as a goal, and cannot be engineered by making the middle tier bad.

Both risks are real: a structure that is too clever will feel like a trick once customers see it; attending only to regulars' feelings may leave all three tiers untouched and the increase unrealised. The middle path is to make 199 solid while giving regulars a transition period with written conditions, rather than using the middle tier as both a decoy and the main product.

The check is an exploratory interview, not a vote: ask five or six regulars to look at two versions of the list, with and without 199, and say which they would choose, why, which entitlement they did not understand, and what is missing now. What is recorded is reasons and sticking points; there is no threshold of "if this many people mention it, add it", and a sample this small cannot justify cutting or adding a tier. The interviews inform the price list; they do not judge anyone's type.
### A classmate's shop asks for pricing help: charge or not
(Fictional scene.) A university classmate has opened a small shop and asks you to look at the price list and the menu structure, saying several times "no rush, whenever you have time".

Either may simply produce a version, and either may ask about scope first. This is closer to a difference in task scope and relationship terms: whether there is time, whether this will recur, and how you and this classmate usually deal with each other all change the approach.

Put the same set of questions to both: how far does this help go, what is delivered, when is it needed, is there a fee, and does a later price change count as a new engagement. One more often checks whether a rule can be applied consistently — free this time, so is it free for the next person who asks; saying "one verbal opinion, implementation billed separately" saves both sides trouble. The other more often starts from the existing relationship — it is not easy for a classmate to ask, so hold the atmosphere first and find a moment to state the boundary. Both reasons can hold at once, and often appear in the same person.
A workable approach is layered: free this time, one verbal opinion, no documents; for implementation, a separate engagement with scope, deliverables, timing and fee written down.

Counterexamples worth remembering: some ENTPs will insist on a simple letter of engagement, and some ESFJs will take on three months of work with "we are classmates". Type does not decide who has better judgement about boundaries; whether the scope can be stated clearly depends on experience, the relationship and the situation. If the two take it on together, divide by who knows how, who has time and who is authorised to speak outward — not by four letters.

body: The most common thing taken as evidence is "who is better at conversation". Both can carry a dinner table, and both can stay silent all evening when tired. Chatting is habit and occasion; the shared E describes direction only, not warmth.

The second is dividing them by "who is better with people". ESFJ can speak very hard when interests are at stake, and ENTP can soothe someone sentence by sentence when it is needed. Treating "good at caring for people" as a type marker is wrong almost every time.

The third is treating seating as rank. Calling ENTP "not grounded" and ESFJ "no opinions of their own" turns a processing order into a defect. Four identical names only mean this writing uses the same vocabulary in a different order; nothing follows about who is better at ideas or more practical, or whose judgement is more reliable.

The fourth is treating J as "likes making plans" and P as "likes changing them". J/P is whether outer life forms an arrangement or keeps options; the same person can build a detailed schedule in a familiar field and improvise in an unfamiliar one, which has more to do with how settled the situation is.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a small shop that has just started to do well, both may strike up conversation with customers, and both may wear a flat expression through an evening of rush orders. The shared E only says attention and energy turn outward more often; it guarantees neither warmth nor remembering names. How much someone chats comes from habit, training and the state of the day.

The difference sits in which face of the same thing gets noticed. One more often looks at what other approaches could work, and whether the structure could flow better; the other more often looks at how the specific people in the room are doing, and how this was handled before. Both kinds of attention appear; the difference is which is taken first more often.

### The price list on the table: both kinds of imagining appear

With the same price list, either may think first on behalf of new customers: how the three tiers differ, whether the middle one is worth it, whether it reads clearly at a glance. Either may also think first on behalf of existing customers: one price has become three, will some feel demoted, and what do we tell the people renewing at the old price. Which side is raised first depends on the role, the information in hand and the last complaint or compliment, with no fixed correspondence to four letters.

What can be compared is the reason. Someone who more often cites "does the choice structure hold up" tends to be calculating tier gaps and looking for anchors; someone who more often cites "will commitments already made be broken" tends to be checking contracts and thinking through a transition. Both reasons can sit in the same discussion, and the same person may raise both in sequence.

The costs sit on both sides. Calculating only the structure may end with existing customers at the door asking "so I have been downgraded?"; attending only to the transition may produce three tiers none of which is worth buying, and the price increase fails. Which side is more likely to go wrong depends on how much of this shop's revenue comes from regulars and whether a price was ever promised, not on anyone's type.

### Why four identical functions read as two different people

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si and ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti. Moving the first two entries to the end gives the other stack: ENTP's Ne is third in ESFJ and Ti fourth; ESFJ's Fe is third in ENTP and Si fourth. The order within each pair stays the same.

The four processes fall into a perceiving group and a judging group. ENTP leads with a perceiving process (Ne), paired with a judging process (Ti). ESFJ leads with a judging process (Fe), paired with a perceiving process (Si). These are positions in the model. They cannot predict the order of actions, creativity or consideration for others.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: some give only the function name for ENTP's Fe and ESFJ's Ne without settling the attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and cannot be used to infer when someone finally thinks of other people. Both base descriptions are the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp) and the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj).

sections.body_md:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same set of services, the same group of regular customers, the same authority and budget, the same launch date. If one person owns the shop and the other was asked for a quick opinion, their different responsibilities can explain which questions they raise.

Align the conditions before reading: the same event, the same information, the same deadline. Both types can use the other's approach; the table contrasts criteria either person could use.

| The same event (one price list, the same regular customers) | ENTP: the basis more likely attended to | ESFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A three-tier draft arrives | Whether the distance between tiers and the choosing path read clearly at a glance | Whether the tier names and wording make regulars feel ranked | Structure and customer comprehension; either can check both |
| What the middle tier adds over the basic one | Would the added service justify the same price difference under consistent criteria across all tiers? | How would that price difference affect regulars who rely on the added service, given what they were promised? | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| A regular says "it was not this price before" | Apply the same transition criteria to customers with comparable purchases | Weigh how the same transition options affect customers who relied on the previous price | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Competitors offer only two tiers | How to explain the differentiation, and which tier serves as the reference | Whether customers will find the options complicated, and whether the wording should be simplified | Positioning and decision cost; either can check with real customer feedback |
| Whether to raise prices across the board | Apply the same viability criteria to the same proposed increases | Weigh how the same increases would affect customers and what was promised to them | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The first week after launch | Keep several ways of responding open while the same launch data comes in | Agree on a provisional date and format for reviewing the same launch data | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. Someone who has priced a shop for years more often calculates the tier gaps first, and the other person touching a price list for the first time may only ask "is this too expensive"; the same person also switches approach depending on how much data is available and how tight the deadline is.
sections.title: ENTP and ESFJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the two passages below are fictional pricing and engagement discussions, covering communication, the organisation of information and the division of work only, not legal, financial or contractual judgement. Real pricing decisions follow your own operating data and professional advice.

When two people work together, friction tends to appear when one is already changing the tiers and the other is still working out how to raise it with regulars. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each handles first. The division can be written down by duty and authority: who owns which part, who has the final signature. Writing it is more reliable than relying on rapport.

### The three tiers: should the middle tier offer less value?

(Fictional scene.) One set of services splits into basic at 99, standard at 199, premium at 399. Early in the discussion someone proposes making 199 visibly poor value, adding only two trivial features over 99, so customers either stay at 99 or jump to 399. The other objects: regulars renewing at a single price are using something close to 199, and turning that into the bad-value tier tells them they have been overpaying for years.

Set the goal first, then the tiers. This time the goal is for most new customers to land on 199: 99 moves volume at thin margin, 399 is a high threshold for a new customer, and the team wants to test whether customers see 199 as good value. With that goal, 199 has to stand up: the added service needs a clear purpose and enough use to justify the price difference of 100; 399 exists as a reference, with clearly wider entitlements and a jump in price, so that 199 looks like the reasonable choice rather than the tier being pushed.

"Will customers move from 199 to 399, and why" is a hypothesis to be tested, known only from the choice distribution and renewal feedback after launch; it cannot be written into the design as a goal, and cannot be engineered by making the middle tier bad.

Both risks are real: a structure that is too clever will feel like a trick once customers see it; attending only to regulars' feelings may leave all three tiers untouched and the increase unrealised. The middle path is to make 199 solid while giving regulars a transition period with written conditions, rather than using the middle tier as both a decoy and the main product.

The check is an exploratory interview, not a vote: ask five or six regulars to look at two versions of the list, with and without 199, and say which they would choose, why, which entitlement they did not understand, and what is missing now. What is recorded is reasons and sticking points; there is no threshold of "if this many people mention it, add it", and a sample this small cannot justify cutting or adding a tier. The interviews inform the price list; they do not judge anyone's type.

### A classmate's shop asks for pricing help: charge or not

(Fictional scene.) A university classmate has opened a small shop and asks you to look at the price list and the menu structure, saying several times "no rush, whenever you have time".

Either may simply produce a version, and either may ask about scope first. This is closer to a difference in task scope and relationship terms: whether there is time, whether this will recur, and how you and this classmate usually deal with each other all change the approach.

Put the same set of questions to both: how far does this help go, what is delivered, when is it needed, is there a fee, and does a later price change count as a new engagement. One more often checks whether a rule can be applied consistently — free this time, so is it free for the next person who asks; saying "one verbal opinion, implementation billed separately" saves both sides trouble. The other more often starts from the existing relationship — it is not easy for a classmate to ask, so hold the atmosphere first and find a moment to state the boundary. Both reasons can hold at once, and often appear in the same person.

A workable approach is layered: free this time, one verbal opinion, no documents; for implementation, a separate engagement with scope, deliverables, timing and fee written down.

Counterexamples worth remembering: some ENTPs will insist on a simple letter of engagement, and some ESFJs will take on three months of work with "we are classmates". Type does not decide who has better judgement about boundaries; whether the scope can be stated clearly depends on experience, the relationship and the situation. If the two take it on together, divide by who knows how, who has time and who is authorised to speak outward — not by four letters.

sections.body_md:
The most common thing taken as evidence is "who is better at conversation". Both can carry a dinner table, and both can stay silent all evening when tired. Chatting is habit and occasion; the shared E describes direction only, not warmth.

The second is dividing them by "who is better with people". ESFJ can speak very hard when interests are at stake, and ENTP can soothe someone sentence by sentence when it is needed. Treating "good at caring for people" as a type marker is wrong almost every time.

The third is treating seating as rank. Calling ENTP "not grounded" and ESFJ "no opinions of their own" turns a processing order into a defect. Four identical names only mean this writing uses the same vocabulary in a different order; nothing follows about who is better at ideas or more practical, or whose judgement is more reliable.

The fourth is treating J as "likes making plans" and P as "likes changing them". J/P is whether outer life forms an arrangement or keeps options; the same person can build a detailed schedule in a familiar field and improvise in an unfamiliar one, which has more to do with how settled the situation is.

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then where you stood when you answered: were you maintaining existing customers or opening new ones during that period, how much information did you have, how tight was the deadline. The pull of a role and a situation is worth recording, but one result cannot establish a stable tendency.

Put the practice in comparable situations: find three or four discussions where you took part in pricing or quoting, and write four lines for each — your role and authority, which pieces of information you had, the questions you asked, and the reason for the trade-off finally adopted. Then add one line: if the duty were different, say from maintaining regulars to opening new customers, would you still choose the same. Use these notes against the four preference definitions above; do not count votes on the first question, and do not label a single reaction with a type.

If the assessment reports dimension scores or preference clarity, check S/N, T/F and J/P by that tool's own notes; without dimension information, record only the two labels and the situation at the time, without inferring "both are possible" or deciding which one is closer to a so-called real type.
sections.title: ENTP and ESFJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Three differ: S/N, T/F and J/P; only E is shared.

S/N compares sourcing: trusting comparable facts and experience, or noticing connections and possibility faster; T/F compares the basis for judgement: impersonal consistency, or people and values; J/P compares outward stance: forming an arrangement, or keeping options. Four identical names in the stack only mean this writing uses the same vocabulary in a different seating; ENTP's Ne and Ti sit third and fourth in ESFJ, and ESFJ's Fe and Si sit third and fourth in ENTP. The three have to be read separately and cannot be packed into "who considers people more, who thinks better".
items.question: Which letters differ, and why do four identical functions read as two different people?

items.answer:
It changes which kind of basis each more often cites first in the same matter: one more often puts possibility and structure on the table first, the other more often puts the people present and existing commitments on the table first.

That easily produces misalignment — one feels "I had not got to that step yet", the other feels "you never mentioned this at all". But who speaks first and which part is covered first depend on role, duty, amount of information and deadline; the same type changes order in different settings, and sequence is not a criterion.
items.question: What does the shifted seating actually change?

items.answer:
Yes, and such counterexamples show that a preference is not a ceiling and does not restrict anyone to one kind of work.

Whether someone can produce a new idea, or smooth a room, depends on training, experience and the relational pressure of the moment. What can be compared is the reason: is this new idea filling a specific gap in front of us, or opening a direction not yet tried; is this smoothing so the discussion can continue, or so that one person does not lose face. Both reasons may appear in the same type, and what matters is how they look across several situations.
items.question: ESFJ comes up with new ideas and ENTP manages the room — are those counterexamples?

items.answer:
By duty, experience and authority, not by four letters.

Whoever knows the costs and customer data better calculates the tier gaps and the reference price; whoever knows the contracts and the regulars better handles the transition and the wording. One person signs off the price, the other's written comments are attached, and a price list signed by both is easier to defend when questioned after launch. If one person holds both kinds of experience, one person can do the whole thing.
items.question: Setting the three tiers together, who fixes the structure and who signs off the price?

items.answer:
Scope and deliverables first, money second; a free verbal opinion and an implementation engagement are costed separately.

One message states four things: how far it goes, what is delivered, when it is needed, and whether there is a fee, plus one line that a later price change counts as a new engagement. For shared expenses such as rent or regular meals, the usual practice applies — for example, flag anything above a certain amount in advance — and that rule has nothing to do with type, nor does it explain who is more willing to spend.

These two labels differ on S/N, T/F and J/P; if the tool reports dimension scores or preference clarity, check by its notes whether all three sit near the boundary. Without dimension information, record only the two labels and the work and relationship situation at the time, without inferring a true or false type, and without concluding from a changing label that "both sets of preferences are available".

The three-tier package, the classmate's request and the regulars' transition are editorial composites, written only to practise discrimination, corresponding to no real business, person or event, and constituting no pricing, contractual or business advice.
